ch09.title: Rebecca's Love
ch09.b002: Jesus was poor, but his social standing in Nazareth was in no way impaired. He was one of the foremost young men of the city, a splendid specimen of robust and intellectual manhood with a reputation as a spiritual leader besides. It was not strange, then, that Rebecca, the eldest daughter of Ezra, a wealthy merchant and trader of Nazareth, should discover that she was slowly falling in love with this son of Joseph. Rebecca first confided her affection to Miriam, Jesus’ sister, and Miriam in turn talked it all over with her mother.
ch09.b003: Mary was intensely aroused. Was she about to lose her son, now become the indispensable head of the family? Would troubles never cease? What could happen next? Then she considered what marriage would mean for Jesus’ future career. Not often, but at least sometimes, she recalled that Jesus was a “child of promise.” After she and Miriam had talked the matter over, they decided to try to stop it before Jesus learned of it. They would go directly to Rebecca, lay the whole story before her, and tell her honestly of their belief that Jesus was a son of destiny, that he was to become a great religious leader, perhaps the Messiah.
ch09.b004: Rebecca listened intently. She was thrilled by the recital and more than ever determined to cast her lot with the man of her choice and to share his career of leadership. Such a man, she argued to herself, would all the more need a faithful and efficient wife. She took Mary’s efforts to dissuade her as the natural dread of a widow about to lose the head and sole support of her family. And knowing that her father approved of her attraction for the carpenter’s son, she reckoned rightly that he would gladly supply the family with an income fully compensating for the loss of Jesus’ earnings. When her father agreed, and when further conferences failed to win Mary and Miriam’s support, she made bold to go directly to Jesus himself.
ch09.b005: The Evening of Her Seventeenth Birthday
ch09.b006: She did this with her father’s co-operation. Ezra invited Jesus to their home for the celebration of Rebecca’s seventeenth birthday. Jesus listened attentively and sympathetically to the recital of these things, first by the father, then by Rebecca herself. He made kindly reply to the effect that no amount of money could take the place of his obligation personally to rear his father’s family, to “⟦Q 127:5.3⟧fulfill the most sacred of all human trusts—loyalty to one’s own flesh and blood.⟦/Q⟧” Ezra was deeply touched by these words of family devotion and withdrew from the conference. His only remark to his wife, Mary, was: “⟦Q 127:5.3⟧We can’t have him for a son; he is too noble for us.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b007: Then began that eventful talk with Rebecca. Until this time Jesus had made little distinction in his association with boys and girls, with young men and young women. His mind had been far too occupied with the pressing problems of practical earthly affairs, and with the intriguing contemplation of his eventual career “about his Father’s business,” ever to have given serious thought to the consummation of personal love in human marriage. But now he stood face to face with another of those problems which every average human being must confront and decide. Indeed was he “⟦Q 127:5.4⟧tested in all points like as you are.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b008: He listened to her attentively, and then he sincerely thanked Rebecca for her expressed admiration, adding, “⟦Q 127:5.5⟧it shall cheer and comfort me all the days of my life.⟦/Q⟧” He explained that he was not free to enter into relations with any woman other than those of simple brotherly regard and pure friendship. He made it clear that his first and paramount duty was the rearing of his father’s family and that he could not consider marriage until that was accomplished. And then he added: “⟦Q 127:5.5⟧If I am a son of destiny, I must not assume obligations of lifelong duration until such a time as my destiny shall be made manifest.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b009: The One Who Went to Sepphoris
ch09.b010: Rebecca was heartbroken. She refused to be comforted, and she importuned her father to leave Nazareth until at last he consented to move to Sepphoris. In the years that followed, to the many men who sought her hand in marriage she had but one answer. She lived for only one purpose: to await the hour when this man, to her the greatest who ever lived, would begin his career as a teacher of living truth.
ch09.b011: And that hour came, and she did not forget. She followed him devotedly through his eventful years of public labor. She was present, unobserved by Jesus, on the day when he rode triumphantly into Jerusalem. And on that fateful and tragic afternoon when the Son of Man hung upon the cross, she stood “among the other women” by the side of Mary, his mother. To her, as well as to countless worlds on high, he was “⟦Q 127:5.6⟧the one altogether lovely and the greatest among ten thousand.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b012: The story of Rebecca’s love for Jesus was whispered about Nazareth and later about Capernaum, so that, although in the years to come many women loved Jesus even as men loved him, never again did he have to reject the personal proffer of another good woman’s devotion. From this time on, human affection for Jesus partook more of the nature of worshipful and adoring regard. But for many years, whenever the story of Jesus’ human personality was told, the devotion of Rebecca was recounted. Miriam, who knew the whole affair and how her brother had forsaken even the love of a beautiful maiden, though she did not understand the factor of his future career, came to idealize Jesus and to love him with a touching and profound affection, as a father as well as a brother.
ch09.b013: A.D. 14, a Passover Without a Lamb
ch09.b014: In his twentieth year, although they could hardly afford it, Jesus felt a strange longing to go up to Jerusalem for the Passover. His mother, knowing of his recent experience with Rebecca, wisely urged him to go. He was not markedly conscious of it, but what he most wanted was a chance to talk with Lazarus and to visit with Martha and Mary. Next to his own family he loved these three most of all. He spent four days going up by way of Megiddo, Antipatris, and Lydda, thinking much about the past events at Megiddo, the international battlefield of Palestine. At Jerusalem he only paused to look upon the temple and the gathering throngs; he had a strange and increasing aversion to this Herod-built temple with its politically appointed priesthood. He passed on to Bethany. Lazarus, the same age as Jesus, was now head of the house, for his mother too had been laid to rest, and Jesus was the idolized ideal of all three.
ch09.b015: On this visit occurred one of those periodic outbreaks of rebellion against tradition, the expression of his resentment toward ceremonial practices which he deemed misrepresentative of his Father in heaven. Not knowing Jesus was coming, Lazarus had arranged to celebrate the Passover with friends in a village down the Jericho road. Jesus now proposed that they keep the feast where they were, at Lazarus’s house. “But,” said Lazarus, “we have no paschal lamb.” Then Jesus entered upon a prolonged and convincing dissertation to the effect that the Father in heaven was not truly concerned with such childlike and meaningless rituals. After solemn and fervent prayer they rose, and Jesus said:
ch09.b017: That evening about twilight these four sat down and partook of the first Passover feast ever celebrated by devout Jews without the paschal lamb. The unleavened bread and the wine had been made ready, and these emblems, which Jesus termed “the bread of life” and “the water of life,” he served to his companions, and they ate in solemn conformity with the teachings just imparted. It became his custom to do this whenever he visited Bethany. When he returned home, he told his mother all about it. She was shocked at first but gradually came to see his viewpoint; nevertheless she was greatly relieved when he assured her that he did not intend to introduce this new idea of the Passover into their family. At home with the children he continued, year by year, to eat the Passover “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧according to the law of Moses.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b019: During this year Mary had a long talk with Jesus about marriage. She asked him frankly whether he would marry if he were free of his family responsibilities. He explained that, since immediate duty forbade his marriage, he had given the subject little thought. He doubted that he would ever enter the marriage state; all such things, he said, must await “my hour,” the time when “my Father’s work must begin.” Having already settled in his mind that he was not to become the father of children in the flesh, he gave very little thought to human marriage. This year he began anew the task of weaving his mortal and divine natures into a simple and effective human individuality, and he continued to grow in moral status and spiritual understanding.
ch09.b020: That year a little help came from the sale of an equity in Capernaum property to a boatbuilder named Zebedee, the last of Joseph’s entire estate. Joseph graduated from the synagogue school and prepared to begin work at the small bench in the home carpenter shop. Though their father’s estate was exhausted, there was now hope that they would fight off poverty, for three of them were regularly at work.
ch09.b021: Jesus was rapidly becoming a man, not just a young man but an adult. He had learned to bear responsibility, to carry on in the face of disappointment, and to bear up bravely when his plans were thwarted and his purposes temporarily defeated. He had learned to be fair and just even in the face of injustice. More and more he depended on the guidance of his heavenly Father while he assumed the fatherly role of guiding the children of his earth family. He was learning, in the words of the record, “⟦Q 127:6.12⟧how to transform the difficulties of time into the triumphs of eternity.⟦/Q⟧”
ch09.b022: He stood now on the threshold of full manhood, rich in the experience of human living, replete in the understanding of human nature, and full of sympathy for its frailties. And all this human experience is an eternal possession of the Universe Sovereign. He is our understanding brother, sympathetic friend, experienced sovereign, and merciful father. And now, as a full-grown man, he prepared to continue his supreme mission of revealing God to men and leading men to God.
ch10.title: The Smithy at Sepphoris
ch10.b002: As Jesus of Nazareth entered upon the early years of his adult life, he was living a normal and average human life on earth. He had chosen this world for his seventh and final bestowal, but otherwise he entered it in a natural manner, growing up as a child of the realm as other mortals do. The twofold purpose of Michael’s bestowal was always before him: to master the experience of living the full life of a human creature in mortal flesh, thereby completing his sovereignty in Nebadon, and to reveal the Universal Father to the mortals of time and space, leading them to a better understanding of that Father.
ch10.b003: Joshua ben Joseph knew full well that he was a man, a mortal man, born of woman, and he chose as his first title the Son of Man. He labored, grew weary, rested, and slept. He was “⟦Q 128:1.2⟧in all things tested, even as you are.⟦/Q⟧” Until after his baptism he availed himself of no supernatural power; as to the attributes of his prehuman existence, he emptied himself, and his knowledge of men and events was wholly self-limited. Yet all these years he was truly divine, a Creator Son of the Paradise Father, and the celestial hosts knew that this man of Nazareth was their beloved Sovereign. A profound suspense pervaded the universe of Nebadon; all celestial eyes were focused on Urantia, on Palestine.
ch10.b004: That spring Jesus took his brother Joseph to the Passover, for having taken James to the temple for consecration, he deemed it his duty to take Joseph as well; he never showed partiality in his family. They went down the Jordan valley and came home by the east Jordan way through Amathus. Joseph asked many leading questions about his brother’s life mission, but to most of them Jesus would only reply, “⟦Q 128:1.15⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧” Still, many words were dropped in those intimate talks that Joseph would remember during the stirring events of later years. As was his custom, Jesus spent the Passover with his three friends at Bethany.
ch10.b006: His brothers and sisters now ranged from seven to eighteen, and Jesus was kept busy helping them through the new awakenings of their intellectual and emotional lives. Simon graduated from school and went to work with Jacob the stone mason, Jesus’ old boyhood playmate and ever-ready defender. In the latter part of the year, when carpenter work was slack about Nazareth, Jesus left James in charge of the repair shop and Joseph at the home bench and went over to Sepphoris to work with a smith. For six months he worked with metals, the ring of hammer on iron filling his days, and he acquired considerable skill at the anvil.
ch10.b007: Before he went, he held one of his periodic family conferences and solemnly installed James, just past eighteen, as acting head of the family. He exacted from each member of the family a formal promise of obedience to James. From that day James assumed full financial responsibility, Jesus making his weekly payments to his brother. Never again did Jesus take the reins out of James’s hands. He could have walked home from Sepphoris every night, but he purposely stayed away, assigning weather and other reasons; his true motive was to train James and Joseph in bearing the family responsibility. He had begun the slow process of weaning his family. Each Sabbath, and sometimes during the week when need arose, he returned to Nazareth to observe the new plan and offer advice.
ch10.b008: Living in Sepphoris gave Jesus a new opportunity to know the gentile viewpoint. He worked with gentiles, lived with gentiles, and made a painstaking study of the gentile mind. But the moral standards of this home city of Herod Antipas were so far below those even of the caravan city of Nazareth that after six months he was not averse to finding an excuse for going home. The group he worked for was about to take up public work in Sepphoris and in the new city of Tiberias, and Jesus was disinclined to have anything to do with employment under Herod Antipas. When he returned to the repair shop, he did not again assume the direction of family affairs. He worked beside James and left him in charge of the home and its budget. By such wise planning Jesus prepared the way for his eventual withdrawal from his family.
ch10.b010: The next year the financial pressure eased a little, for four were at work. Miriam earned considerable by selling milk and butter, and Martha had become an expert weaver. More than a third of the repair shop was paid for. Jesus stopped work for three weeks, the longest rest from daily toil since his father’s death, to take Simon to Jerusalem for the Passover. They went by way of the Decapolis and returned by the coast road through Joppa and Caesarea, a journey that acquainted Jesus with nearly the whole of Palestine north of Jerusalem.
ch10.b011: At Philadelphia they met a merchant from Damascus who took such a liking to the two brothers that he insisted they stay at his Jerusalem headquarters. While Simon attended the temple, Jesus spent much of his time talking with this well-educated and much-traveled man. He owned over four thousand caravan camels and had interests all over the Roman world. He proposed that Jesus come to Damascus and enter his Oriental import business, but Jesus said he did not feel justified in going so far from his family just then. Yet on the way home he thought much about the distant cities and the remote countries of the Far West and the Far East of which he had so often heard caravan travelers speak.
ch10.b012: While Simon was received into the commonwealth of Israel, Jesus mingled with the throngs and had many conferences with gentile proselytes. The most notable was with a young Hellenist named Stephen, on his first visit to Jerusalem. On Thursday afternoon of Passover week, as both strolled about viewing the Asmonean palace, Jesus began a casual conversation that led to a four-hour discussion of the way of life and the true God and his worship. Stephen never forgot his words. This was the same Stephen who later believed the gospel and was stoned to death by irate Jews, and some of his extraordinary boldness came directly from this interview. Yet he never surmised that the Galilean he had talked with some fifteen years before was the very one he proclaimed the world’s Savior. When he yielded up his life, there stood by one named Saul, a citizen of Tarsus, and what Saul saw that day eventually led him to become the aggressive and indomitable Paul.
ch10.b013: On the way home Simon and Jesus had many heart-to-heart talks as they prepared their meals by the wayside, and Simon felt he had begun to know his father-brother. He kept the family up late relating his experiences. Mary was much upset to hear that Jesus had spent most of his time in Jerusalem “⟦Q 128:3.8⟧visiting with the strangers, especially those from the far countries.⟦/Q⟧” Seldom now did anyone speak of his future mission, and Mary was slowly giving up the idea, though at times her faith revived when she recalled the visit of Gabriel.
ch10.b015: The last four months of that year Jesus spent in Damascus as the guest of the merchant he had met at Philadelphia, whose representative had sought him out in Nazareth. This part-Jewish merchant proposed to devote an extraordinary sum to a school of religious philosophy at Damascus, a center of learning to out-rival Alexandria, and he proposed that Jesus begin at once a long tour of the world’s educational centers in preparation for becoming its head. This was one of the greatest temptations Jesus ever faced in the course of his purely human career. Presently the merchant brought before him twelve merchants and bankers who agreed to support the school. Jesus showed deep interest and helped them plan its organization, but he always expressed the fear that his other, unstated but prior obligations would prevent his accepting the direction of so pretentious an enterprise.
ch10.b016: His would-be benefactor was persistent. He employed Jesus at his home doing translating, while he, his wife, and their sons and daughters sought to prevail upon him. But Jesus would not consent. He knew that his mission on earth was not to be supported by institutions of learning, and that he must not obligate himself in the least to be directed by the “councils of men,” however well-intentioned. He who was later rejected by the religious leaders of Jerusalem was hailed as a master teacher by the businessmen and bankers of Damascus while he was still an obscure carpenter of Nazareth.
ch10.b017: He never spoke of this offer to his family, and the end of the year found him back in Nazareth at his daily duties as if he had never been tempted. Nor did those men of Damascus ever connect the later citizen of Capernaum who turned all Jewry upside down with the carpenter who had refused the honor their wealth could procure. Jesus intentionally kept the episodes of his life apart so that they would never be associated as the doings of one individual. He did not want later generations to venerate the teacher in place of obeying the truth he lived and taught. He did not want men to believe in him unless their hearts responded to the spiritual realities revealed in his teachings.
ch10.b019: This was Jesus’ first year of comparative freedom from family responsibility, for James managed the home well with his counsel and help. The week after the Passover a young man from Alexandria came to Nazareth to arrange a meeting, and in the middle of June Jesus went over to Caesarea to meet five prominent Jews of Alexandria. They besought him to establish himself in their city as a religious teacher, offering to begin with the position of assistant to the chazan in their chief synagogue. They warned that any uprising in Palestine would be national suicide: Rome would crush it in three months, and Jerusalem and its temple would be destroyed, not one stone left upon another.
ch10.b020: Jesus listened to all they had to say, thanked them for their confidence, and, in declining, in substance said, “⟦Q 128:1.15⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧” They were nonplused by his apparent indifference. Before leaving, they presented him with a purse in token of their esteem and in compensation for his time and expense. But he refused the money too, saying: “⟦Q 128:5.4⟧The house of Joseph has never received alms, and we cannot eat another’s bread as long as I have strong arms and my brothers can labor.⟦/Q⟧”
ch10.b021: The rest of that year was the most uneventful six months of his whole career. He communed much with his Father in heaven and made tremendous progress in the mastery of his human mind. But in December James confided that he was in love with Esta, a young woman of Nazareth. Jesus consented to their marriage two years later, provided James had meanwhile trained Joseph to direct the home. Emboldened, Miriam came with her own plans: Jacob, the younger stone mason, once Jesus’ self-appointed champion, had long sought her hand. Jesus promised his blessing as soon as she felt Martha was competent to take her place as eldest daughter.
ch10.b023: The twenty-fifth year began with the family in good health and their finances in the best condition since Joseph’s estate disappeared. The repair shop was fully paid for; they owed no man. Jesus decided to take Jude, just graduated from the synagogue school, on his first visit to the temple. They went by the Jordan valley, for Jesus feared trouble if he took his hot-tempered and patriotic young brother through Samaria. In Jerusalem, on their way to the temple, they met Lazarus, and while Jesus was arranging their joint Passover, a Roman guard close by made improper remarks about a passing Jewish girl. Jude flushed with fiery indignation and told the soldier so. The guard promptly arrested him, and before Jesus could caution him with a glance, Jude poured out a voluble denunciation of his pent-up anti-Roman feelings. Jude, with Jesus beside him, was taken at once to the military prison.
ch10.b024: Jesus failed to obtain either a hearing or a release in time for the Passover that evening, and since the next day was a “holy convocation,” even the Romans would not hear charges against a Jew. So Jude remained in confinement until the morning of the second day, and Jesus stayed at the prison with him. Then Jesus appeared before the military magistrate. By apologizing for his brother’s youth and judiciously explaining the provocation, he so handled the case that the magistrate allowed the young Jew some excuse. In dismissing them he said to Jesus: “⟦Q 128:6.7⟧You had better keep your eye on the lad; he’s liable to make a lot of trouble for all of you.⟦/Q⟧” And the Roman judge spoke the truth.
ch10.b025: They walked over to Bethany for the night to explain why they had missed the Passover supper. Jesus did not tell the family of the arrest, but some three weeks after their return he had a long talk with Jude, after which Jude told them himself. He never forgot the patience and forbearance his brother-father had shown. This was the last Passover Jesus attended with any member of his own family. That year his meditations were often interrupted by Ruth and her playmates, and he was always ready to set aside the contemplation of his future work to share their joy. Beside the repair shop he provided sand, blocks, and stones, and the bolder children would peek in and say, “⟦Q 128:6.11⟧Uncle Joshua, come out and tell us a big story.⟦/Q⟧” Then they would tug him out to his favorite rock by the corner of the shop and sit in a semicircle before him, the smallest climbing on his knees. The children loved Jesus, and Jesus loved the children.
ch10.b027: As his twenty-sixth year began, Jesus became strongly conscious that he possessed a wide range of potential power, but he was fully persuaded that it was not to be used by the Son of Man until his hour should come. The conclusion of his thinking was once expressed in his prayer on the hilltop: “⟦Q 128:7.2⟧Regardless of who I am and what power I may or may not wield, I always have been, and always will be, subject to the will of my Paradise Father.⟦/Q⟧” Family affairs ran smoothly except for Jude, who would not settle down to work. James and Joseph favored casting him out, but Jesus counseled: “⟦Q 128:7.4⟧Be patient. Be wise in your counsel and eloquent in your lives, that your young brother may first know the better way and then be constrained to follow you in it.⟦/Q⟧” When Jude ran away to the fishermen at the lake and Simon brought him home, Jesus took him to Magdala and placed him with a relative who was a fisherman, and from then on Jude worked fairly well.
ch10.b028: Mary sensed that her son was making ready to leave them. Leave them to go where? To do what? She could not fathom her first-born son. In November a double wedding took place: James married Esta, and Miriam married Jacob. Even Mary was happy, except when she remembered that Jesus was preparing to go away. Joseph was formally installed as head of the family, and Jude, the day after the wedding, assured Joseph that he could depend on him “⟦Q 128:7.11⟧to do my full duty, and more if it is needed.⟦/Q⟧” And he kept his promise.
ch10.b029: The day after the wedding Jesus held an important conference with James. He told him confidentially that he was preparing to leave home. He gave James full title to the repair shop, formally abdicated as head of Joseph’s house, and most touchingly established his brother as “⟦Q 128:7.13⟧head and protector of my father’s house.⟦/Q⟧” They signed a secret compact by which James assumed full financial responsibility for the family. Then Jesus said: “⟦Q 128:7.13⟧But, my son, I will continue to send you something each month until my hour shall have come, but what I send shall be used by you as the occasion demands.⟦/Q⟧” And so Jesus made ready to enter the second, home-detached phase of his adult life before his public entrance upon his Father’s business.
ch11.title: The Day He Left Home
ch11.b002: Jesus had now fully and finally separated himself from the management of the Nazareth household and from the direction of its members. He would continue, right up to his baptism, to contribute to the family finances and to take a keen interest in the spiritual welfare of each of his brothers and sisters, and he was always ready to do everything humanly possible for the comfort and happiness of his widowed mother. But the Son of Man had made every preparation for detaching himself permanently from the Nazareth home, and this was not easy for him. He loved his family, and this natural affection had been tremendously augmented by his extraordinary devotion to them. The more fully we bestow ourselves upon our fellows, the more we come to love them, and Jesus had given himself to his family without reserve. For more than four years they had discerned that he was planning for this separation; the sadness of it was tempered only by the gradual way he had prepared them.
ch11.b003: Then, in January of A.D. 21, on a rainy Sunday morning, he took unceremonious leave of his family. The rain fell softly on the flat roofs and the narrow lanes of the hillside town as he explained only that he was going over to Tiberias and then on a visit to other cities about the Sea of Galilee. And so he left them, never again to be a regular member of that household. He spent a week at Tiberias, the new city soon to succeed Sepphoris as the capital of Galilee, and, finding little there to interest him, he passed on through Magdala and Bethsaida to Capernaum, where he stopped to visit his father’s friend Zebedee.
ch11.b005: Zebedee was a boatbuilder, and his sons were fishermen. He had long known of the skill of the Nazareth craftsman, who was expert in both designing and building and a master at working with wood. For a long time Zebedee had been thinking of making improved boats; he now laid his plans before Jesus and invited him to join the enterprise, and Jesus readily consented. He worked with Zebedee only a little more than a year, but in that time he created a new style of boat and established entirely new methods of boatmaking. By superior technique and greatly improved methods of steaming the boards, they began to build craft far safer for sailing the lake than the older types. For years Zebedee had more work than his small establishment could handle, and within five years practically every boat on the lake had come from his shop at Capernaum. Jesus became well known among the Galilean fisherfolk as the designer of the new boats.
ch11.b006: Zebedee’s shops stood on the lake south of Capernaum, and his home lay down the shore near the fishing headquarters of Bethsaida. Jesus lived in his home during the year and more he remained, and having long worked alone in the world without a father, he greatly enjoyed this period of working with a father-partner. Zebedee’s wife, Salome, a relative of Annas, the former high priest at Jerusalem, became a great admirer of Jesus. She loved him as she loved her own sons, James, John, and David, and her four daughters looked upon him as their elder brother. Jesus often went fishing with the three sons, and they learned that he was an experienced fisherman as well as an expert boatbuilder.
ch11.b007: All this year Jesus sent money each month to James. He returned to Nazareth in October for Martha’s wedding, and after that he was not in Nazareth again for over two years. Frequently he went down to the caravan station, for Capernaum lay on the direct route from Damascus to the south. Capernaum was also a strong Roman military post, and its commanding officer was a gentile believer in Yahweh, “a devout man,” as the Jews called such proselytes. This officer, of a wealthy Roman family, had built a beautiful synagogue and presented it to the Jews a short time before Jesus came. Jesus conducted the services in this new synagogue more than half the time that year, and some of the caravan people who chanced to attend remembered him as the carpenter from Nazareth. When it came to paying taxes, he registered himself as a “skilled craftsman of Capernaum,” and from that day to the end of his earth life he was known as a resident of Capernaum.
ch11.b008: In the synagogue library chests he found many new books, and he spent at least five evenings a week in intense study. One evening he gave to social life with the older folks and one to the young people. There was something gracious and inspiring about him that invariably drew young people; perhaps his secret was that he was always interested in what they were doing, while he seldom offered advice unless they asked for it. The Zebedee family almost worshiped him, and they never missed the question-and-answer conferences he held each evening after supper before going to the synagogue to study. He talked freely about politics, sociology, science, and philosophy, but never presumed to speak with authoritative finality except when discussing religion, the relation of man to God.
ch11.b009: Once a week he met with the entire household, shop, and shore helpers, for Zebedee had many employees. It was among these workers that Jesus was first called “the Master.” They all loved him. He enjoyed his labors at Capernaum, but he missed the children playing out by the side of the Nazareth carpenter shop. Frequently Jude came over on the Sabbath to hear him speak in the synagogue, and the more he saw of his eldest brother, the more he became convinced that Jesus was a truly great man. That year Jesus made great advances in the mastery of his human mind and attained new levels of conscious contact with his indwelling Thought Adjuster. It was the last year of his settled life. Never again did he spend a whole year in one place or at one undertaking.
ch11.b011: In March of A.D. 22 Jesus took leave of Zebedee and of Capernaum, asking only for a small sum to pay his way to Jerusalem. He agreed to stay in Jerusalem until the Passover, and the Zebedee family all promised to come and keep the Passover supper with him. They all sorrowed when he left, especially Zebedee’s daughters.
ch11.b012: Before leaving, he had a long talk with his new-found friend and close companion, John Zebedee. He told John that he contemplated traveling extensively until “my hour shall come,” and asked him to send some money to the family at Nazareth each month until the funds due him were exhausted. And John made him this promise:
ch11.b014: After Jesus had gone, John consulted his father and was surprised to find how large a sum was due Jesus. Since the matter had been left entirely in their hands, they decided to invest it in property and use the income for the family. Zebedee knew of a little mortgaged house in Capernaum that was for sale, and John bought it with Jesus’ money, holding the title in trust for his friend. The rent was applied to the mortgage, and with a large fund Jesus later sent and a little help from Zebedee, John paid off the remainder and secured clear title to the two-room house. So Jesus became the owner of a house in Capernaum, though no one had told him. The family at Nazareth, knowing nothing of this, believed the time had come to manage without his help, and James, remembering his contract, assumed full responsibility for them with the help of his brothers.
ch11.b016: For almost two months Jesus spent most of his time in Jerusalem listening to the temple discussions, with occasional visits to the schools of the rabbis; most Sabbaths he spent at Bethany. He carried a letter from Salome introducing him to the former high priest Annas as “⟦Q 129:2.7⟧one, the same as my own son.⟦/Q⟧” Annas spent much time with him and personally took him to visit the many academies of the Jerusalem teachers. Jesus thoroughly inspected these schools and observed their methods, but he never asked a single question in public. Annas regarded him as a great man, yet he was puzzled how to advise him: it would be foolish to suggest he enter the schools as a student, yet, untrained in them, he could never be accorded the status of a regular teacher. Then the Passover drew near, and with the throngs from every quarter came Zebedee and his entire family from Capernaum. They all stayed at the spacious home of Annas and celebrated the Passover together as one happy family.
ch11.b017: A Father and Son from India
ch11.b018: Before the end of that Passover week, by apparent chance, Jesus met a wealthy traveler and his son, a young man of about seventeen. They came from India and were on their way to visit Rome and other points on the Mediterranean. They had planned to arrive in Jerusalem at the Passover, hoping to find someone to engage as interpreter for both of them and tutor for the son. The father insisted that Jesus travel with them. Jesus told him about his family and said it hardly seemed fair to go away for almost two years, during which they might find themselves in need. The traveler from the Orient then proposed to advance him the wages of one year, so that he could entrust the funds to friends to safeguard his family against want. And Jesus agreed to make the trip.
ch11.b019: He turned this large sum over to John Zebedee, and it was this money that John applied to the mortgage on the Capernaum house. Jesus took Zebedee fully into his confidence about the Mediterranean journey but enjoined him to tell no man, not even his own flesh and blood, and Zebedee never disclosed his knowledge of Jesus’ whereabouts during the nearly two years that followed. Before Jesus returned, the family at Nazareth had just about given him up as dead; only the assurances of Zebedee, who went up to Nazareth several times with John, kept hope alive in Mary’s heart. The family got along well in that time. Jude increased his share, and each month, as Jesus had instructed him, John Zebedee took presents to Mary and Ruth.
ch11.b020: Throughout the tour Jesus was known as the Damascus scribe, though at Corinth and other stops on the return he was known as the Jewish tutor. He never revealed this phase of his life to any member of his family nor to any of the apostles. Some of his friends thought he had gone back to Damascus, others to India, and his family believed he was in Alexandria, since they knew he had once been invited there. When he returned, he did nothing to change their opinion. Only Zebedee knew the facts, and Zebedee told no one. Jesus was consistently careful not to build up an overattractive and attention-consuming personal career; he wanted to make no unusual or overpowering appeals to his fellow men.
ch11.b022: The real purpose of this journey around the Mediterranean was to know men. He came very close to hundreds of human beings, and he met and loved all manner of men, rich and poor, high and low, black and white, educated and uneducated, religious and irreligious, moral and immoral. Through this travel-training he completed his contact with the diverse peoples of his day, and by the time he came home he had just about learned how man lived and wrought out his existence on Urantia. On the journey he made great advances in mastering the material mind, and his Adjuster made great progress in its spiritual conquest. By the end of the tour Jesus virtually knew, with all human certainty, that he was a Son of God, a Creator Son of the Universal Father. Little by little the Adjuster brought up in his mind shadowy memories of his Paradise existence, and the last of them, his farewell conference with Immanuel of Salvington, would become clear on the very day of his baptism in the Jordan.
ch11.b023: To the onlooking celestial intelligences this Mediterranean trip was the most enthralling of all his earth experiences up to the crucifixion. He was still the carpenter of Nazareth, the boatbuilder of Capernaum, the scribe of Damascus; he was still the Son of Man, a man among men. He experienced the whole range of human emotion. He was a child of joy and a being of rare good humor; likewise was he a “⟦Q 129:4.4⟧man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.⟦/Q⟧” He did not come to Urantia to be a detailed example for every man or woman to copy. He lived his mortal life by the same means by which all of us may live ours; and as he lived it in his day and as he was, so he set the example for us to live our lives in our day and as we are. Jesus is “⟦Q 129:4.7⟧the new and living way from man to God, from the partial to the perfect, from the earthly to the heavenly, from time to eternity.⟦/Q⟧” By the end of his twenty-ninth year he had virtually finished the living of the life required of mortals in the flesh. He came on earth the fullness of God to be manifest to man; he had now become well-nigh the perfection of man awaiting the occasion to become manifest to God. And he did all of this before he was thirty years of age.
